notes: PARTIALLY PINNED. The runtime closure is pinned byte for byte: every wheel below is named, sized and hashed from pypi.org, resolved for windows-x86_64-cp313 -- the platform this was first tested on. The DPDFNet model is DECLARED BUT NOT HASHED: the machine that wrote this manifest could not reach huggingface.co, so the model's size and digest are recorded at install time from what the publisher actually serves, and its revision is the publisher's branch rather than an immutable commit. That is a weaker claim than the closure's and the difference is worth stating: an artifact with a digest here is checked against a number this repository committed to, and one without is checked against the digest its publisher reports at install time. Both refuse a file that arrives wrong; only the first refuses a publisher who changed their mind. A stage in that state carries "provisional": true, the settings row says so in words, and `python tools/pin_pipeline_models.py --stage dpdfnet --revision <sha>` on a machine that can reach the hub turns the first claim into the second. LavaSR cannot be offered as a managed download -- its weights are on a host this manifest's machine could not reach to pin -- but it is installable from a folder somebody fills themselves, and its runtime closure carries its code. See its own entry.

runtime.closure_notes: The enhancement runtime is deliberately NOT PocketTTS's interpreter (section 14.6). Lifecycle coupling does not imply dependency coupling: Pocket's closure stays reproducible, the pipeline can later serve Kokoro and Sopro, and a pipeline update cannot mutate the environment a working voice depends on. The closure below is the ONNX path -- Path A of section 10.4 -- which is the one to validate first because it shares a runtime with DPDFNet and gives explicit thread control. If Phase 0 rejects it, section 14.5 says to use the official PyTorch/Vocos LavaSR in this same isolated runtime with a project-owned rate adapter, which is a different closure and a different 'build' number here, not a different design. The ONNX Runtime wheel is the DirectML build rather than the plain CPU one, and that is a deliberate choice of ONE closure over two. The DirectML wheel carries the CPU execution provider as well as the DirectML one, so the placement setting picks a provider inside an installed runtime instead of picking between two installed runtimes -- no second interpreter, no second download, and a machine with no usable graphics card still runs every stage exactly as it did. The cost is honest and small: the DirectML build's newest release is 1.24.4 where the CPU-only build is at 1.29.0, and it declares sympy, which the CPU build no longer does. DirectML rather than CUDA because one wheel and no CUDA toolkit covers every Direct3D 12 card, where the CUDA build would need a toolkit matched per card generation -- the same wheel serves a 30-series and a 50-series card, which the CUDA builds do not.

stages.label: DPDFNet
stages.summary: Cleans noise and synthesis artifacts out of generated speech, at whatever rate it is given.
stages.attribution: DPDFNet by Ceva. Model dpdfnet8_48khz_hr from the publisher's own repository.

contract.notes: Measured from upstream 0.6.0's own source rather than from its README. StreamEnhancer.process(chunk, sample_rate=N) resamples N to the model's native rate internally and returns output back at N, so the stage is handed Pocket's real 24000 Hz and gives back 24000 Hz -- output_rate is null because this stage's output rate is its caller's, and the 48 kHz in the model name is the network's own working rate. The streaming path is a causal STFT that upstream documents as deliberately NOT bit-identical to its offline enhance(); that is the correct path for real time and is the one this feature uses. onnx_path is passed explicitly so resolve_model() never reaches the network (I-VP-22).

stages.label: LavaSR
stages.summary: Restores speech bandwidth and delivers 48 kHz.

contract.notes: MEASURED, from upstream's own source rather than its README, and this settles the question the whole design was gated on. LavaSR/model.py's enhance() resamples 16000 -> 48000 UNCONDITIONALLY, in both the denoise and the no-denoise branch: `torchaudio.functional.resample(wav, 16000, 48000)`. load_audio() will happily load a file at some other input_sr, but enhance() still interprets whatever it is given as 16 kHz -- so handing it Pocket's 24 kHz would stretch the reply by half and nothing would say so. The README's '8-48 kHz input' describes the project's ambition, not this code path. So the adapter's contract is: resample the real source rate to 16000 deterministically, run the model, take 48000 out. That is what mc_voice_pipeline_runtime hands the worker and what LavaStage implements; THE WINDOW IS DERIVED FROM THE MERGE RATHER THAN CHOSEN FOR LATENCY, which is the correction to leaving analysis_ms and context_ms null. FastLRMerge -- upstream's Linkwitz-inspired blend of the original low band with the upsampled high one -- takes an rfft of the WHOLE block it is handed, and its transition is a fixed *bin* count (1024) rather than a fixed width in Hz. So the width of the crossover in Hz is set by how long the window is, and a short window does not merely cost quality, it moves the crossover: a 60 ms block puts the fade at 0-16522 Hz, where it clips at DC and the merge is simply wrong; 100 ms puts it at 2879-13115 Hz, blending three kilohertz of real speech into the guess; 350 ms puts it at 6536-9462 Hz, which is a sane crossover around the 8000 Hz cutoff the adapter sets from backend_rate // 2. The block is analysis_ms + 2*context_ms, so 250 + 2*50 = 350 ms, and anything under about 64 ms of block is below the floor where a listening test would even be measuring what it thought it was. What is still judgement rather than arithmetic is the trade the other way: first_output_samples is analysis + context = 300 ms of intrinsic latency, which fits inside the browser's own 0.7 s start buffer and so costs nothing visible in the common case. A longer window narrows the crossover and a shorter one widens it; where on that curve this should sit is what the latency-quality sweep in section 10.7 is for. These are the floor it should start from, not its conclusion.

torch.closure_notes:
THE PYTORCH FLAVOUR, AND IT CARRIES ONNX RUNTIME TOO -- deliberately, because that is what keeps this to ONE PROCESS. LavaSR upstream is a PyTorch model and DPDFNet is an ONNX one; running them in two runtimes would mean two workers, two job objects and two ways to leak a process that outlives the voice it belongs to. Carrying both wheel sets in one interpreter costs 126 MB over the ONNX closure and buys back every containment guarantee unchanged -- the same start and stop path, the same Windows job object, the same pdeathsig, the same coupling to PocketTTS's residency. A stage's backend chooses which interpreter the single contained worker runs, never how many workers there are.

SO IT CARRIES DPDFNET'S OWN PACKAGE TOO, AND THAT IS THE POINT OF THE PARAGRAPH ABOVE RATHER THAN AN EXTRA. Carrying ONNX Runtime is not the same as carrying the stage that uses it: DPDFNet imports `dpdfnet`, and this closure had the runtime and not the package. The effect was that enabling BOTH stages was worse than enabling either -- one worker serves the pair, the pair means this closure, and the worker died on `import dpdfnet` before a sample reached either model. Every reply came out unenhanced, with a ModuleNotFoundError in the log and both stages showing Installed and Enabled on the panel. soxr comes with it, because librosa resamples through it, and soundfile is the win_amd64 wheel the ONNX closure pins rather than the pure one, because only that build carries libsndfile beside it. Whatever the ONNX closure needs to run DPDFNet, this one needs too.

CPU ONLY, AND THAT IS NOT A DESIGN CHOICE. torch on PyPI for Windows is the CPU build; every CUDA dependency in its metadata is gated behind platform_system == "Linux", and the Windows CUDA wheels live on download.pytorch.org, which the machine that wrote this manifest could not reach. A CUDA closure is a second platform entry here, resolved and hashed the same way, from a machine that can reach that host. Until then a card cannot be offered for the torch backend, and the settings row says so rather than showing a control that would do nothing.

THREE PACKAGES ARRIVE AS SOURCE, NOT WHEELS. LavaSR publishes no wheel, its vocos dependency is a fork pinned to a git branch, and encodec ships an sdist only -- and vocos imports encodec unconditionally, so all three are needed to import any of them. All three are pure Python, so installing them is lifting one named package directory onto the path: no build step runs and no setup.py is executed. Only the named directory is taken, because a GitHub tarball is a repository rather than a distribution and carries tests, training scripts and, in encodec's case, four megabytes of sample audio. encodec is pinned by digest here; the two GitHub tarballs are pinned to immutable commits but arrive against the digest codeload serves, because the machine that wrote this manifest cannot reach that host.
